analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare Advantage plans to speed up and publicly report their prior authorization decisions.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 70 of 102 senators cosponsoring from both parties, the bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee since May 2025 with no action taken.
analysis.plain_summary: Millions of seniors in Medicare Advantage plans need their insurer's advance approval — 'prior authorization' — before getting care like imaging, surgery, or home health, and waits or denials can delay treatment. This bill would force those plans to use a standardized electronic approval system, tell the public how often they deny requests and how long they take, disclose when they use artificial intelligence to make decisions, and let the government set deadlines for responses. It would not ban prior authorization; plans could still say no, but in the open and on the clock.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans, who would see faster, more consistent approval decisions and could look up each plan's denial and appeal rates before choosing coverage. Doctors and suppliers also benefit from a single electronic process instead of faxes and proprietary portals.

how_it_helps.text: Medicare Advantage plans that use prior authorization must establish an electronic prior authorization program meeting federal standards — faxes, plain electronic forms, and proprietary portals that don't meet standards would no longer count.

Plans must report annually, for public posting on a CMS website plan by plan, what services they subject to prior authorization, their initial approval and denial rates, how often denials are appealed and overturned, average and median response times in hours, and how often they used AI or automated decision technology.
The bill lets the Secretary of Health and Human Services set binding response deadlines for prior authorization decisions, such as 24 hours, on top of the existing 72-hour standard.

Plans must adopt enrollee protection standards, including waiving or easing prior authorization for providers with a track record of compliance, and reviewing annually which services actually need prior authorization with input from enrollees and providers.

Enrollees can request the criteria a plan uses to make prior authorization decisions, and CMS and the health IT coordinator must report on whether routinely approved services could move to real-time decisions and how AI-driven denials affect patient access, especially in rural and low-income communities.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurers bear the cost of building compliant electronic systems and publishing detailed annual data, and they lose the ability to operate prior authorization opaquely. Those costs could show up partly in premiums or trimmed extra benefits, and until CMS writes the standards, enrollees still face the same denials.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not limit when plans can use prior authorization or override a denial — plans keep full discretion to deny care; the bill's protections depend heavily on standards and deadlines that the Secretary and CMS would have to write later through rulemaking.

The main protections do not start until plan years 2027 and 2028, and oversight arrives as reports years later — a GAO evaluation is not due until 2032 — so relief for seniors would be slow even if enacted.

Plans face significant new reporting and technology obligations covering every covered item and service except Part D drugs, and critics of MA regulation generally warn such compliance costs tend to be passed along through premiums or reduced supplemental benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors, the gains are real but indirect: more transparency about which plans deny care most, faster electronic processing, and possible binding deadlines — yet the bill leaves prior authorization itself fully intact and defers the teeth to future regulations. The cost falls on the insurers in compliance and disclosure, which is modest relative to the size of the Medicare Advantage market, though some could trickle to enrollees. A bill that had also directly restricted denials would do more; this one mainly shines light and speeds paperwork.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has not scheduled it for any action since.

narrative.text: Sen. Roger Marshall introduced the bill on May 20, 2025, joined by 48 other senators from both parties.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day, where it has remained with no further action in the record.
The bill has since drawn 70 cosponsors — 37 of 45 Senate Democrats, 32 of 55 Senate Republicans, and 1 of 2 independents — a majority of the chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage insurers are better off so far: they keep prior authorization decisions — and the data about their denial rates — out of public view and free of federal electronic and timeliness standards while the bill waits in committee.

sides.party_line_note: Support spans both parties heavily: 37 of 45 Senate Democrats and 32 of 55 Senate Republicans have cosponsored, and the original 49 included senators from both caucuses; no senator has opposed it on the record.

industries.note: The bill would force plans to build standardized electronic prior authorization systems and publish plan-level data on denial rates, appeal overturns, response times, and AI use — exposing a process they now run largely out of public view. They keep prior authorization itself and their gatekeeping role, but lose opacity and face possible binding response deadlines set by the Secretary.

Doctors and suppliers would get one standardized electronic process instead of faxes and payer-specific portals, access to each plan's approval criteria upfront, and possible waivers from prior authorization based on their compliance track record.

industries.industry: Health IT and electronic prior authorization vendors
industries.note: The mandate that every MA plan use standards-compliant electronic prior authorization transmissions creates a compliance market for software vendors in that space.

analysis.trajectory: With 70 of 102 senators cosponsoring, the bill is unlikely to die for lack of support, but Finance has not moved it in months. The most realistic path is being folded into a larger Medicare or year-end health package rather than receiving its own vote; bills like it have cleared one chamber in past Congresses without becoming law, so committee inaction remains the biggest risk.
